questions.stem_html:
A 71-year-old woman with decompensated heart failure receives intravenous loop diuretics for 3 days. Her dyspnea improves, but a moderate unilateral pleural effusion persists. Pleural fluid protein is 3.3 g/dL, serum protein is 6.0 g/dL, pleural LDH is 150 U/L, and serum LDH is 230 U/L. The serum-to-pleural albumin gradient is 1.4 g/dL. Cultures and cytology are negative.

Why can this hydrostatic effusion satisfy exudative Light criteria after treatment?

options.text_html: Diuretics increase pleural capillary permeability through direct endothelial toxicity
Removal of water from the pleural space concentrates protein and lactate dehydrogenase
Reduced lymphatic drainage causes selective accumulation of immunoglobulins
Bacterial enzymes raise pleural LDH despite sterile culture
Hepatic albumin synthesis falls enough to reverse the protein gradient

questions.explanation_html: Diuresis removes relatively protein-poor water faster than pleural proteins leave, concentrating pleural protein and LDH. The resulting pseudoexudate can meet Light criteria despite a transudative cause. A serum-to-pleural albumin gradient greater than about 1.2 g/dL supports a transudative hydrostatic process when diuresis has concentrated pleural fluid.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Loop diuretics do not convert a transudate to an inflammatory exudate by injuring pleural capillaries.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Impaired lymphatic drainage can cause an exudate, but it does not explain the temporal association with aggressive diuresis and a large albumin gradient.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: There are no infectious findings, and bacterial metabolism is not required for a pseudoexudate.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Reduced serum albumin would not selectively concentrate pleural protein and is inconsistent with the measured albumin gradient.

questions.educational_objective: Explain why heart-failure effusions may become pseudoexudates after diuresis and use the serum-to-pleural albumin gradient to recover the underlying transudative physiology.
